about.title: Albany Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Albany's mix of small businesses along Solano and San Pablo, plus warehouses and job sites tucked near the I-80 corridor, means workplace injuries here range from repetitive strain in retail settings to falls and equipment accidents in industrial spaces. In California, workers' compensation is generally your only path against your employer, no matter who was at fault. But that's not the whole story: if a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or even another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim outside the workers' comp system. Alameda County workers navigating a job injury often don't realize both paths might apply to their situation. LawProactive doesn't practice law or charge fees; we simply connect injured Albany workers with an independent attorney who can look at the facts, explain your options plainly, and help you understand what deadlines apply to your specific case.

whyChoose.title: Why Albany Workers Consider Getting Legal Advice

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California law generally makes workers' comp your exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can open a separate claim worth exploring.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: You typically have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and missing that window can complicate your claim before it even starts.

items.title: Retaliation Is Against the Law
items.desc: Employers cannot legally punish you for reporting an injury or pursuing a claim, and an attorney can help you understand your protections if you're worried about your job.

items.question: I was hurt on a jobsite near San Pablo Avenue. Do I file workers' comp or a lawsuit?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' comp is your primary route against your employer regardless of fault. But if a third party, like a contractor or equipment supplier, contributed to the accident, you may also have a separate injury claim. An attorney can look at the details of your Albany jobsite incident and explain which paths apply.

items.question: How long do I have to act after a workplace injury in Albany?
items.answer: You generally need to notify your employer within 30 days of the injury to preserve your workers' comp rights. If a third-party claim applies, California law generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file that separate claim. Because these deadlines run differently, it helps to get clarity early.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for reporting an injury?
items.answer: No, retaliation for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim is illegal under California law. If you're facing pressure or pushback after an injury near I-80 or anywhere else in Albany, an independent attorney can help you understand your rights and next steps.
